\chapter{Welcoming a Guest}
\label{ch:hi-welcoming-a-guest}
\hlchaptermodality{51}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name what a Hindi household puts in front of a guest at the door.}

Complete HI-C51-sweet and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[phūl]{\hi{फूल} (phūl) — a flower}

\label{lesson:HI-C51-flower}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{āśīrvād} mean, and what did \emph{praṇām} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{फूल}}
\textbf{\hi{फूल}} (\emph{phūl}) — \textquotedblleft{}a flower\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{phulla}, 'blossomed, opened out', from \emph{phull-}, 'to bloom'. So the Hindi word for a flower is at bottom a word for the act of opening, with the object named after the event.

The double \emph{ll} collapsed and paid for itself by lengthening the vowel in front of it, which is the standard trade in this family — the same bargain that gave you \hi{कान} out of \emph{karṇa}. It is also the measure of lightness: something that weighs nothing at all is \emph{phūl jaisā}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things at a welcome.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{phūl}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{phūl}, then \emph{praṇām}, the flower and the bow at the door
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{फूल} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a flower\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mālā]{\hi{माला} (mālā) — a garland}

\label{lesson:HI-C51-garland}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{phūl} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{माला}}
\textbf{\hi{माला}} (\emph{mālā}) — \textquotedblleft{}a garland\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{mālā}, a garland or a string of beads, and the second sense has travelled furthest: the string of a hundred and eight beads counted through the fingers is a \emph{mālā}, and English borrowed the word back, unchanged, for that same object.

Around the neck of a guest it is a welcome. Around the frame of a photograph it is mourning. The object does not change at all; where it is hung decides everything.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: a flower and a garland made of them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mālā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{mālā}, then \emph{phūl}, the string and the thing it is made of
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{माला} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a garland\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āṁgan]{\hi{आँगन} (āṁgan) — a courtyard}

\label{lesson:HI-C51-courtyard}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{mālā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{आँगन}}
\textbf{\hi{आँगन}} (\emph{āṁgan}) — \textquotedblleft{}a courtyard\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{aṅgaṇa}, the open ground a house encloses — the room with no roof over it. Old town houses are built around one, and a great deal of what English would put in a living room happens there instead: the drying, the talking, the sitting with a guest.

The mark above the line marks a nasal that used to be a whole consonant, exactly as it does in \emph{uṅglī}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and this one is where you seat the guest.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{āṁgan}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{āṁgan}, then \emph{mālā}, then \emph{phūl}, back down the run
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{आँगन} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a courtyard\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mez]{\hi{मेज़} (mez) — a table}

\label{lesson:HI-C51-table}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{āṁgan} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{मेज़}}
\textbf{\hi{मेज़}} (\emph{mez}) — \textquotedblleft{}a table\textquotedblright{}.

Persian \emph{mez}, and behind the Persian sits Portuguese \emph{mesa}, out of Latin \emph{mēnsa}. Portuguese ships carried the object and its name into the Indian Ocean, which is the same route that brought \hi{कमरा} in from \emph{camera}.

There was no inherited word for a raised surface on four legs because the household had not had one; people ate and wrote and worked at floor level. The word arrived with the furniture, which is usually how that happens.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and one of them came off a ship.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mez}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{mez}, then \emph{āṁgan}, one of them standing inside the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{मेज़} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a table\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[miṭhāī]{\hi{मिठाई} (miṭhāī) — a sweet}

\label{lesson:HI-C51-sweet}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{mez} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{मिठाई}}
\textbf{\hi{मिठाई}} (\emph{miṭhāī}) — \textquotedblleft{}a sweet\textquotedblright{}.

From \emph{mīṭhā}, 'sweet', with the \emph{-āī} ending that turns a quality into a thing you can hold — sweetness first, then the sweet itself. Behind \emph{mīṭhā} is Sanskrit \emph{miṣṭa}, 'sweetened, relished'.

Nothing closes a welcome better: the garland at the door, the seat in the courtyard, and something sweet in the hand before anybody says why they have come.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five, and the run is closed: a flower, a garland, a courtyard, a table, a sweet.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{miṭhāī}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{phūl}, \emph{mālā}, \emph{āṁgan}, \emph{mez}, \emph{miṭhāī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{मिठाई} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a sweet\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
